prompt.context: Your client is an entrepreneur looking to invest in a new bar. He needs to determine how profitable the company will be and convince his primary investor, his father, that it will be a viable business.
prompt.question: What factors would you consider and investigate to determine the profitability of this sports bar and convince the father-investor that it is a viable business?

clarifying_info.q: What does the average customer spend on food per visit?
What does the average customer spend on drinks per visit?

clarifying_info.a: Kitchen (when open): 4 people at $10/hr; Bar: 1 person at $5/hr; Wait Staff: 3 people at $5/hr
Food has a 20% gross margin (80% cost); Drinks have a 50% gross margin (50% cost)

clarifying_info.q: Are there other cost details available?
clarifying_info.a: No specific data on utilities, legal, insurance, licenses, training, remodeling, equipment, and other startup costs

clarifying_info.q: How many customers does the bar serve?
clarifying_info.a: (Refer to Exhibit 1 — give when asked about customer volumes)

exhibits.title: Market Research — Customer Traffic by Day and Time
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down food and drinks customers per hour across two day segments (12pm–8pm and 8pm–12am/2am) and two day groupings (Sunday–Wednesday and Thursday–Saturday)

framework: Revenue: Break down by food vs. drinks; average spend per customer; volume of customers by day-part and day type
COGS: Food cost (80% of food revenue) and drinks cost (50% of drinks revenue)
Labor: Kitchen, bar, and wait staff headcount and hourly wages across day and night shifts
Fixed Costs: Lease ($10,000/month); note other fixed costs (utilities, marketing, insurance, licenses) are not fully specified
Profitability: Weekly and annual profit after all costs
Investment Perspective: Compare annual profit to start-up capital; calculate break-even and ROI for the father-investor

questions.prompt: Calculate the total weekly food and drink orders using Exhibit 1
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a structured table separating Sun-Wed (4 days) from Thu-Sat (3 days), and day from night within each segment. Sun-Wed day: 10 food/hr x 8 hrs = 80 food orders, 4 drinks/hr x 8 hrs = 32 drink orders. Sun-Wed night: 4 food/hr x 4 hrs = 16 food orders, 15 drinks/hr x 4 hrs = 60 drink orders. Daily totals Sun-Wed: 96 food, 92 drinks. Weekly (x4 days): 384 food, 368 drinks. Thu-Sat day: 15 food/hr x 8 hrs = 120 food orders, 5 drinks/hr x 8 hrs = 40 drink orders. Thu-Sat night: 5 food/hr x 6 hrs = 30 food orders, 20 drinks/hr x 6 hrs = 120 drink orders. Daily totals Thu-Sat: 150 food, 160 drinks. Weekly (x3 days): 450 food, 480 drinks. Total weekly: 834 food orders, 848 drink orders.

math.setup: Separate Sun-Wed (4 days, 8 day hrs + 4 night hrs) from Thu-Sat (3 days, 8 day hrs + 6 night hrs); multiply orders/hr by hours then by days
steps: Sun-Wed food day: 10 x 8 = 80; night: 4 x 4 = 16; daily = 96; weekly = 96 x 4 = 384
Sun-Wed drinks day: 4 x 8 = 32; night: 15 x 4 = 60; daily = 92; weekly = 92 x 4 = 368
Thu-Sat food day: 15 x 8 = 120; night: 5 x 6 = 30; daily = 150; weekly = 150 x 3 = 450
Thu-Sat drinks day: 5 x 8 = 40; night: 20 x 6 = 120; daily = 160; weekly = 160 x 3 = 480
math.answer: 834 weekly food orders; 848 weekly drink orders

questions.prompt: Calculate weekly revenue and weekly COGS for food and drinks
questions.guidance: Weekly revenue = price x weekly orders. Food: $15 x 834 = $12,510. Drinks: $20 x 848 = $16,960. Total weekly revenue = $29,470. COGS: Food gross margin is 20%, so food cost = 80% of food revenue = $12,510 x 0.88 = ~$11,009. Drinks gross margin is 50%, so drinks cost = 50% of drinks revenue = $16,960 x 0.50 = $8,480. Total weekly COGS = $19,489.

math.setup: Weekly revenue = price x weekly orders; weekly COGS = (1 - gross margin) x weekly revenue

questions.guidance: Kitchen: 4 people x $10/hr. Bar: 1 person x $5/hr. Wait staff: 3 people x $5/hr. Sun-Wed: 4 days x 12 hours (12pm-12am) = 48 hours per staff type. Thu-Sat: 3 days x 14 hours (12pm-2am) = 42 hours per staff type. Total hours = 48 + 42 = 90 hours per week per staff type. Kitchen labor: 4 x $10 x 90 = $3,600. Bar labor: 1 x $5 x 90 = $450. Wait staff labor: 3 x $5 x 90 = $1,350. Total weekly labor = $5,400.

math.setup: For each staff category: (headcount) x (hourly wage) x (total weekly hours); hours = Sun-Wed hours + Thu-Sat hours
steps: Sun-Wed hours: 4 days x 12 hrs/day = 48 hrs
Thu-Sat hours: 3 days x 14 hrs/day = 42 hrs
Total weekly hours per category: 48 + 42 = 90 hrs

questions.guidance: Weekly lease = $10,000 / 4 weeks = $2,500. Weekly profit = $29,470 (revenue) - $19,489 (COGS) - $5,400 (labor) - $2,500 (lease) = $2,081. Annual profit = $2,081 x 50 weeks = $104,050. Key takeaway: business is not projected to lose money, but cost assumptions are likely incomplete (utilities, marketing, etc. excluded).

math.setup: Weekly profit = weekly revenue - weekly COGS - weekly labor - weekly lease; annual profit = weekly profit x 50 weeks

questions.prompt: The client estimates start-up capital of $500K (renovations, equipment, licenses). How long to break even? What is the 5-year ROI? (Assume no interest)
questions.guidance: Break-even = $500,000 / $104,050 = ~4.8 years. 5-year ROI = ((104,050 x 5) - 500,000) / 500,000 = (520,250 - 500,000) / 500,000 = 20,250 / 500,000 = ~4.1%. Interviewer note: this is less than 1% per year. Strong candidates will note the father could likely find a better return elsewhere and that the margin is thin relative to initial investment.

math.setup: Break-even = up-front costs / annual profit; 5-yr ROI = ((annual profit x 5) - up-front costs) / up-front costs

brainstorming.prompt: What risks or additional cost factors should the client and his father consider that are not captured in the base model?

categories.name: Startup / Capital Risks
ideas: Licensing and permits (potentially costly and time-consuming)
Cost of purchasing used vs. new equipment to reduce upfront capital

categories.name: Revenue & Market Risks
ideas: Location quality and foot traffic vs. competitors
Customer attrition after initial novelty wears off
Seasonality and sporting event calendar dependency
Ability to build brand loyalty and charge higher margins over time

categories.name: External / Macro Risks
ideas: Sudden increase in food COGS (food shortage, supply chain)
Minimum wage increases raising labor costs
New competitors entering the local market

categories.name: Revenue Upside Opportunities
ideas: Different operating model emphasis (food-focused vs. drink-focused)

recommendation: The sports bar is projected to be profitable at approximately $104K per year, clearing break-even on $500K start-up capital in roughly 4.8 years

However, the 5-year ROI of only 4.1% (~0.8%/year) is very thin; the father-investor should compare this against alternative investments (e.g., index funds, real estate) that may offer faster payback and higher returns
If the client proceeds, reducing up-front capital (used equipment, modest redesign) and adding revenue streams (events, advertising, sponsorships) would materially improve the investment case
risks: Several cost categories (utilities, marketing, insurance, legal) are excluded from the model — actual profitability is likely lower than $104K
Thin annual margins leave the business highly vulnerable to wage increases, food cost spikes, or a drop in customer volume
4.8-year break-even assumes steady weekly performance with no revenue shortfalls or unexpected expenses
next_steps: Incorporate utilities, marketing, and insurance costs into the profitability model for a more accurate picture
Investigate ways to shorten break-even: reduce start-up costs through used equipment or simpler renovation
Explore additional revenue streams (events, jukebox, advertising) to improve margin
Research alternative investments so the father can benchmark this opportunity against the market
